The crystal structure of the periplasmic ribose binding protein of the <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=ABC-28-CPLX">ribose ABC transporter</a> showed it to bind (and thus presumably to facilitate transport of) <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-1110">&beta;-D-ribopyranose</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1583688">Mowbray92a</a>]. <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD0-1110">&beta;-D-ribopyranose</a> is the most common form of ribose in solution, about 60% [<a href="http://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0008621598000408">Drew98</a>].
<p>
The enzyme <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=EG10817-MONOMER">D-ribose pyranase</a> accelerates the conversion between the pyranose and furanose forms of &beta;-D-ribose.  Interconversion of the &alpha;- and &beta;-anomers of D-ribofuranose is fast and spontaneous [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15060078">Ryu04</a>].
<p>
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.7.1.15">EC 2.7.1.15, ribokinase</a>, has been shown to be specific to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-10330">&alpha;-D-ribofuranose</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9519409">Sigrell98</a>], which it converts to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-15318">&alpha;-D-ribose 5-phosphate</a>, an intermediate of the pentose phosphate pathway, and hence it flows through the pathways of central metabolism to satisfy the cell's need for precursor metabolites, reducing power, and metabolic energy.
<p>
Review: Mayer, C. and W. Boos, Hexose/Pentose and Hexitol/Pentitol Metabolism. EcoSal Module 3.4.1 [<a href="http://www.ecosal.org/">EcoSal</a>]</comment>

<comment datatype="string">RbsACB is a high affinity ribose uptake system that is a member of the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) superfamily of transporters.
<p>
Early studies characterized mutants that were defective in a high-affinity ribose transport system and characterized genes of the <i>rbs</i> region including <i>rbsB, rbsA</i> and <i>rbsC</i> which encode a periplasmic ribose binding protein (RbsB) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/339843">Galloway77</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7035438">Garwin82</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6313683">Groarke83</a>], a putative ATP-binding subunit (RbsA) and a putative inner membrane protein (RbsC) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6327617">Iida84</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6327616">Lopilato84</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3011793">Bell86</a>]. Active RbsAC<sub>2</sub>B complexes have been reconstituted in liposomes; RbsAC<sub>2</sub>B, RbsAC and RbsBC complexes can be purified by varying cofactor additions and are suggestive of a transport cycle with the following characteristics: RbsA-ATP-Mg<sup>2+</sup> binds to ribose loaded RbsBC; ATP hydrolysis results in ribose release and dissociation of RbsB from RbsAC; ADP dissociation from RbsAC causes RbsA to dissociate which allows loaded RbsB to again bind RbsC [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25533465">Clifton15</a>].
<p>
<i>rbsACB</i> is part of a larger operon - <i>rbsDACBKR</i> - which includes both regulatory and structural genes involved in ribose utilization; expression is subject to glucose repression mediated by CRP-cAMP; expression is negatively regulated by the the transcription factor <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=PD03867">RbsR</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6327616">Lopilato84</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6327617">Iida84</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15520470">Zheng04</a>] 
<p>
</comment>

<comment datatype="string">RbsA is the ATP-binding subunit of a high affinity ribose uptake system; RbsA contains a signature motifs conserved in  ATP-binding cassette (ABC) proteins; RbsA contains an ABC-ABC domain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3086314">Buckel86</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9593292">Linton98</a>]</comment>

<comment datatype="string">The transcription factor RbsR, for "<b>R</b>i<b>b</b>o<b>s</b>e <b>R</b>epressor," is negatively autoregulated and controls the transcription of the operon involved in ribose catabolism and transport [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1304369">Mauzy92</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6327616">Lopilato84</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11750821">Laikova01</a>]. Transcription of this operon is induced when <i>E. coli</i> is grown in the absence of glucose and when the physiological inducer D-ribose binds to the RbsR repressor [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11750821">Laikova01</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3011793">Bell86</a>]. When D-ribose binds to RbsR, the protein becomes inactive because the binding affinity of RbsR decreases [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1304369">Mauzy92</a>].
<p>
RbsR represses not only the <i>rbs</i> operon for transport and utilization of D-ribose but also the <i>de novo</i> synthesis of purine nucleotides from D-ribose 5-phosphate. In the presence of the inducer D-ribose, RbsR activates the salvage pathway of purine nucleotide synthesis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23651393">Shimada13</a>].
<p>
Although little is known about the mechanism of regulation of the RbsR transcription factor, Mauzy et al. in 1992 demonstrated that this regulator acts as a repressor by binding to <i>cis</i>-acting elements, which have a conserved inverted repeat sequence and overlap the <i>rbsD</i> promoter [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1304369">Mauzy92</a>]. 
<p>
RbsR belongs to the GalR/LacI family, which forms a bundle of four helices characteristic of proteins of an HTH DNA contact motif. The C-terminal 270 residues of RbsR are homologous to the ribose-binding protein RbsB</comment>
